## Dataset -- research question -- design

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\begin{minipage}[t][1.0cm][t]{\linewidth}\textbf{One-sample t-test / Paired t-test - one-sample t-test on difference (Captopril)}\end{minipage}
\begin{itemize}
\item Is there an effect of administering captopril on the blood pressure of patients with hypertension?
\item 15 persons at random
\item blood pressure before and after treatment on the same patient (pretest/posttest, paired measurements)
\end{itemize}
$\Rightarrow$ difference $Y=\text{BP}_\text{after}-\text{BP}_\text{before}$.
}{
\begin{minipage}[t][1.0cm][t]{\linewidth}\textbf{Two-sample t-test (Armpit microbiome)}\end{minipage}
\begin{itemize}
\item
Is there an effect of microbiome transplantation on the relative abundance of \textit{Staphylococcus}?
\item 20 persons at random
\item divided over 2 \textbf{independent} groups (10 placebo, 10 transplantation).
\end{itemize}
}
```

## Translating the research question into an effect size in the population

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\[\delta=\mu-\mu_0\]
\begin{itemize}
\item difference between the population mean $\mu$ and a prespecified value $\mu_0$
\item for captopril / paired data
\begin{itemize}
\item  $\mu$: average difference after - before in the population
\item $\mu_0=0$
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
}{
\[\delta = \mu_1-\mu_2\]
\begin{itemize}
\item difference between group means
\end{itemize}
}
```

## Point estimator

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\[\hat\delta = \hat{\mu} - \mu_0, \quad\quad\hat\mu=\bar Y\]
}{
\[\hat\delta=\hat\mu_1-\hat\mu_2=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_2\]
}
```

## Model / distribution

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\begin{eqnarray*}
Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2) &\Longrightarrow& \bar Y\sim N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
\end{eqnarray*}
}{
\begin{eqnarray*}
Y_{ij}\sim N(\mu_j,\sigma^2)&\Longrightarrow& \bar Y_{j} \sim N\left(\mu_j,\frac{\sigma^2}{n_j}\right)\\
&\Longrightarrow& \bar Y_1-\bar Y_2\sim N\!\left(\mu_1-\mu_2,\ \sigma^2\left(\tfrac1{n_1}+\tfrac1{n_2}\right)\right)
\end{eqnarray*}
}
```

## Assumptions

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\begin{itemize}
\item Representative sample: $E[\bar Y]=\mu$
\item Normality
\item Independence (between subjects)
\end{itemize}
}{
\begin{itemize}
\item Representative sample: $E[\bar Y_j]=\mu_j$
\item Normality
\item Independence \textbf{and} equal variances between the 2 groups ($\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\sigma^2$)
\end{itemize}
}
```

## Variance/SE estimator

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\begin{minipage}[t][1.3cm][c]{\linewidth}\centering$\hat\sigma^2=S^2=\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y)^2}{n-1}$\end{minipage}
\begin{minipage}[t][1.0cm][c]{\linewidth}\centering$SE_{\bar Y}=\dfrac{S}{\sqrt n}$\end{minipage}
}{
\begin{minipage}[t][1.3cm][c]{\linewidth}\centering$S_p^2=\dfrac{\sum_{j=1}^2\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}(Y_{ij}-\bar Y_j)^2}{n_1+n_2-2}$\end{minipage}
\begin{minipage}[t][1.0cm][c]{\linewidth}\centering$SE_{\bar Y_1-\bar Y_2}=S_p\sqrt{\tfrac1{n_1}+\tfrac1{n_2}}$\end{minipage}
}
```

## Pivotal statistic

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\[T=\frac{\bar Y-\mu}{SE_{\bar Y}}\sim t_{n-1}\]
}{
\[T=\frac{(\bar Y_1-\bar Y_2)-(\mu_1-\mu_2)}{SE_{\bar Y_1-\bar Y_2}}\sim t_{n_1+n_2-2}\]
}
```

## Confidence interval

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\[\bar Y\pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\,SE_{\bar Y}\]
}{
\[(\bar Y_1-\bar Y_2)\pm t_{n_1+n_2-2,\alpha/2}\,SE_{\bar Y_1-\bar Y_2}\]
}
```

## Hypothesis test

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\[H_0:\mu=\mu_0 \quad\text{vs}\quad H_1:\mu\neq\mu_0\]
(or one-sided: $\mu<\mu_0$ or $\mu>\mu_0$)

\vspace{0.4cm}

Test statistic under $H_0$:
\[T=\frac{\bar Y-\mu_0}{SE_{\bar Y}}\sim t_{n-1}\]
for captopril $\mu_0 =0$
}{
\[H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0 \quad\text{vs}\quad H_1:\mu_1-\mu_2\neq0\]
(or one-sided: $\mu_1-\mu_2<0$ or $\mu_1-\mu_2>0$)

\vspace{0.4cm}

Test statistic under $H_0$:
\[T=\frac{\bar Y_1-\bar Y_2}{SE_{\bar Y_1-\bar Y_2}}\sim t_{n_1+n_2-2}\]
}
```

\begin{itemize}
\item Both statistics are a \textbf{signal-to-noise ratio}: $T=\hat\delta/SE_{\hat\delta}$, with $\hat\delta=\bar Y-\mu_0$ (one-sample) and $\hat\delta=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_2$ (two-sample). 
\item The p-value is the probability to obtain, under the null hypothesis ($H_0$), in a random sample with the same design, a test statistic that is as extreme or more extreme than the one observed in the experiment (more extreme $\rightarrow$ in the direction of $H_1$).
\end{itemize}

## R function

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\texttt{t.test(x, mu = mu0)}\\
or paired: \texttt{t.test(x1, x2, paired = TRUE)}
}{
\texttt{t.test(y \textasciitilde{} group, var.equal = TRUE)}
}
```

## When the assumptions are not met

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\begin{itemize}
\item No normality, large $n$: central limit theorem
\item No normality, small $n$: permutation test (permute the sign of $Y-\mu_0$, $2^n$ possibilities)
\end{itemize}
}{
\begin{itemize}
\item Unequal variances: Welch two-sample t-test
\item No normality, large $n$ in both groups: central limit theorem
\item No normality, small $n$: nonparametric test (Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney, Chapter 9)
\end{itemize}
}
```

## Design aspects: what does the power depend on?

```{=latex}
\twocol{
\begin{minipage}[t][1.4cm][c]{\linewidth}\centering$T=\dfrac{\bar Y-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt n}$\end{minipage}
\begin{itemize}
\item $S$: not under our control, depends on the variability in the population
\item $n$: most important design parameter
\item significance level (usually 5\%)
\item true effect size $\mu-\mu_0$: not under our control, so we have to assess it upfront to determine the minimal $n$ needed to pick up the minimal effect size $\delta$ that is scientifically relevant.
\end{itemize}
}{
\begin{minipage}[t][1.4cm][c]{\linewidth}\centering$T=\dfrac{\bar Y_1-\bar Y_2}{S_p\sqrt{\tfrac1{n_1}+\tfrac1{n_2}}}$\end{minipage}
\begin{itemize}
\item $S_p$: not under our control, depends on the variability in the population
\item $n_1,n_2$: most important design parameters; for a fixed total $n_1+n_2$ the $SE$ is minimal when $n_1=n_2$
\item significance level (usually 5\%)
\item true effect size $\mu_1-\mu_2$: not under our control, so we have to assess it upfront to determine the minimal $n$ needed to pick up the minimal effect size $\delta$ that is scientifically relevant.
\end{itemize}
}
```
